stories.title: Police exhume body of former Czechoslovak foreign minister Jan Masaryk
stories.summary: The top diplomat was found dead on March 10, 1948, in the courtyard beneath his bathroom window, supposedly after a fall. Police said their probe aims to settle questions that have surrounded the death ever since.
stories.article_text_excerpt: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5KPEk Some historians believe Jan Masaryk, seen as a pro-Western figure, may have been killed by Soviet agents Image: AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement Czech police said Wednesday they had begun exhuming the remains of former Czechoslovak Foreign Minister Jan Masaryk in an attempt to clear up speculation surrounding his death nearly 80 years ago. In a statement posted to X, police said they planned to examine the remains, buried at Prague 's Olsany Cemetery, "using the most modern forensic methods." "We believe that today's actions will bring us closer to clarifying the circumstances leading to the death of Jan Masaryk," the statement said. What happened to the former top diplomat? Masaryk was found dead on March 10, 1948, dressed only in his pajamas, in the courtyard at the Foreign Ministry beneath his bathroom window. The mysterious circumstances surrounding his death, at the height of the Cold War , have fueled speculation for decades. At the time, the Interior Ministry claimed that he had committed suicide. Others believed his fall may have been an accident, or that he was murdered by Soviet agents

stories.title: Ratko Mladic, the man behind Srebrenica massacre, dies at 84
stories.summary: For many, Ratko Mladic represented the horrors of the Bosnian war. He was convicted of genocide for the Srebrenica massacre and other war crimes. On Thursday, he died in detention at The Hague.
stories.article_text_excerpt: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5JWvb Ratko Mladic, seen here in April 1993, was later found responsible for some of the most serious war crimes committed during the Bosnian war Image: Chris Helgren/REUTERS Advertisement More than 30 years after the end of the 1992-1995 war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Srebrenica remains emblematic of its brutality. And no one is more closely linked to the genocide that took place in the small town in eastern Bosnia than Ratko Mladic , the former commander-in-chief of the Bosnian Serb army. Although the United Nations had declared Srebrenica a "safe area," Bosnian Serb forces attacked the town. Within just a few days in July 1995, they expelled women and children, then killed more than 8,300 unarmed Muslim boys and men in the nearby village of Potocari — on Mladic's direct orders, according to the verdict handed down by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) in The Hague 22 years later. At the time, Srebrenica was the largest massacre in Europe since World War II . The ICTY classified it as genocide. The early morning raid on Villena Museum in eastern Spain lasted just a few minutes. A group of thieves described by one official as "super-fast and super-professional" made off with almost the entire Treasure of Villena collection, leaving behind only a few items. What happened in the heist? stories.article_text_excerpt: Slovenia’s parliament on Wednesday allowed prosecutors to pursue a criminal case against former Prime Minister Robert Golob over allegations that he improperly meddled in police staffing after taking office in 2022. All 75 lawmakers present — including Golob himself — voted against granting him parliamentary immunity, allowing proceedings to move forward. The decision was taken without debate or explanations of the voting. Golob had already told parliament he would not invoke immunity and wanted the case resolved as quickly as possible. Advertisement Advertisement The corruption case stems from allegations by Golob’s former Interior Minister Tatjana Bobnar, who said he pressured her to make personnel changes inside the police. Bobnar resigned in December 2022 and subsequently reported the alleged pressure to prosecutors and Slovenia’s anti-corruption commission. Golob has denied wrongdoing. Ljubljana’s District Court opened a judicial investigation in October 2025. Prosecutors had to ask parliament to lift Golob’s immunity after he was elected as an MP this year. Golob’s liberal Freedom Movement remains Slovenia’s largest opposition party .

stories.article_text_excerpt: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5HIpq Sea cucumbers are neither cucumbers nor fish, but invertebrate marine animals with a skin or hard covering Image: oceansasia.org Advertisement When it comes to smuggling, squishy sea blobs that spend their lives eating and pooping are probably not what comes to mind. But a group of lumpen creatures known as sea cucumbers are at the center of a $200 million (€175 million) black market trade. Known alternately and misleadingly as sea cucumbers or sand fish, they are actually neither cucumbers nor fish, but echinoderms. In other words, invertebrate marine animals with a skin or a hard covering. Found in abundance around the Andaman Islands — the easternmost landmass of the Indian territory — local biologist Sangamesh Uday said they are so ecologically important that without them the intertidal zone "wouldn't be an ecosystem, it would just be broken rocks." stories.article_text_excerpt: Nearly 5% of goods entering the EU are fake, costing businesses an estimated €83 billion annually. At the port of Alicante, OLAF and Spanish Customs officers sift through shipping containers, hunting for counterfeit products hidden in plain sight among legitimate trade. Experts describe illicit trade as a sophisticated global business model, no longer limited to luxury items but now spanning car parts, electronics, pharmaceuticals and food. Counterfeit car components pose particular risks, as they bypass safety testing entirely. Officials stress that buying fakes helps finance serious crimes, including drug and human trafficking, urging shoppers to think twice before chasing a bargain.

stories.article_text_excerpt: A car bomb exploded in front of a police station in Mexico on Sunday night, wounding six people, authorities said.The blast happened in the town of Ojocaliente in Zacatecas, a state with key routes for drug trafficking."The explosive was placed in a private vehicle and caused physical damage to the station and properties located nearby," state government secretary Rodrigo Reyes said in a post on Facebook."Six civilians have been reported wounded, who are receiving medical care," he said in an earlier post.Zacatecas is key to the drug trade because it links central Mexico with the north and west of the country and features routes that are key to smuggling cocaine and other narcotics to the United States.Horrific drug violence plagued the state for years, with bodies turning up and people going missing almost on a daily basis until relative calm set in.But in July, five bodies appeared hanging from a bridge in the town of Pozos de Gamboa, about 75 kilometres from Ojocaliente.The victims included a former mayor, civil servants and business people from other parts of the state.
